summary: Discusses architectural implications of Network Address Translation and gives guidelines for implementations. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Network Address Translation (NAT) maps addresses between networks and can let multiple private hosts share public address space. The translation can also disrupt applications and security mechanisms that expect addresses to remain unchanged end to end.

questions: why does nat break the internet
subtitle: An analysis of the architectural trade-offs created by network address translation.

tldr.problem: Network Address Translation can ease IPv4 address pressure, but changing packet addresses and keeping connection state affects end-to-end communication.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC examines NAT's benefits and costs, including address mapping, application gateways, stateful failure points, protocol compatibility and deployment choices.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC presents architectural analysis and deployment cautions. It does not define a new NAT protocol.

today: RFC 2993 is an Informational document published in November 2000, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It analyzes NAT's architectural effects and gives deployment guidelines.

sections.title: What NAT Changes
sections.content:
Network Address Translation (NAT) maps IP addresses from one address administration to another. Network Address Port Translation (NAPT) also maps transport identifiers so several endpoints can share one public IP address.

The RFC frames the architectural concern around end-to-end communication: endpoints should control communication, while the network moves packets between them. A NAT changes packet headers and keeps mapping state inside the network, so it is not transparent to every application.
sections.plainLanguage: NAT changes addresses as packets cross a network boundary. Applications that depend on the original address may notice that change.

sections.title: Why Networks Use NAT
sections.content:
The RFC describes several benefits. NAT can hide internal address changes when a provider changes, and dynamic mappings can reuse globally routable addresses for intermittent access customers.

NAPT can allow multiple endpoints to share one public address. NAT also blocks inbound connections unless they are administratively mapped, similar to packet-filtering firewalls. These benefits explain its appeal, but they do not remove its costs.
sections.plainLanguage: NAT can reduce the number of public addresses a network needs and can simplify changes to its provider connection. Incoming connections need an explicit mapping.

sections.title: Effects on Applications and Reliability
sections.content:
Some applications include IP addresses or ports inside their data. NAT may not know how to update those fields, so an application-specific gateway may be needed for each affected protocol. If no suitable gateway exists, the application may fail across the translator.

A NAT also keeps connection mappings. If it fails, traffic using those mappings fails; redundant NAT devices need consistent shared state and compatible paths. These requirements can make troubleshooting and failover more difficult than with stateless packet forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: An application may send an address inside its message, where a basic translator cannot change it. A translator failure can also interrupt connections whose state it holds.

sections.title: Security and IPv6 Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC warns that NAT can create an impression of security without the managed policy of a firewall. It also says NAT can interfere with IPsec because IP address changes can invalidate authentication, and a DNS application gateway that edits signed records can conflict with DNSSEC.

The document discusses NAT's effect on IPv6 transition. It says NAT can extend IPv4 address use and can assist some IPv6 transition approaches, while IPv6-to-IPv4 translation faces the same architectural issues as NAT. These are the RFC's analysis and expectations at publication.
sections.plainLanguage: NAT is not a replacement for an intentionally configured firewall. Changing addresses can also break security checks that rely on the original packet headers.

sections.title: Questions to Consider Before Deployment
sections.content:
The deployment guidance asks operators to examine name resolution, static or dynamic mappings, single versus redundant translators, and which applications need to cross the NAT. For dynamic mappings, it recommends DNS responses with a time to live of zero so clients do not retain stale addresses.

Operators should also consider inbound services, encrypted payloads, secure DNS, and address collisions when VPNs connect private networks. The RFC presents these points as cautions for planning a NAT deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: Before deployment, check how addresses and names will be mapped and which applications depend on them. Redundant translators and connected private networks need careful planning.
